The additional low-Mach comparison uses the same analytic family with consistently scaled pressure and density, comparing ordinary Roe with a dissipation-preconditioned Roe flux. Open the additional low-Mach vortex verification KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits KEEP stands for kinetic-energy and entropy preserving. The work of Yuichi Kuya, Kosuke Totani, and Soshi Kawai at Tohoku University seeks a low-dissipation balance between the conservative equations of compressible flow. The original 2018 paper is the starting point. The authors’ 2022 conference explanation, especially §2.2 and Eq. (9), states the Cartesian flux implemented here. This exhibit implements the original second-order arithmetic-mean Cartesian flux, with periodic boundaries and classical RK4. It does not implement every later scheme named KEEP. Watch its smooth-vortex evolution. Which quantities should be preserved?# In a smooth periodic inviscid flow, mass, momentum, and total energy are conservative. The total kinetic energy alone is generally not constant in compressible flow: pressure work exchanges kinetic and internal energy. With K = integral rho |u|²/2, dKdt=∫p ∇⋅u dV.dtdK​=∫p∇⋅udV. A kinetic-energy-consistent convective discretization should not create a spurious kinetic-energy source through an inconsistent mass/momentum product rule. This is different from imposing dK/dt = 0 on a compressible vortex. We measure the dimensionless entropy proxy S∗=∫ρlog⁡(pργ)dV.S∗​=∫ρlog(ργp​)dV. For a fixed ideal-gas composition this differs from physical entropy only by fixed factors and an additive mass term. Its change per initial mass is useful when initial isentropic data give S_* approximately zero; dividing by initial S_* would be ill-conditioned. For the grid update formula, see the semidiscrete update and two-point flux. The implementation is a central two-point flux-difference method of second spatial order. It has no Riemann-solver dissipation. 1. This explains the cross-pressure term and the cross-velocity kinetic term in the implemented flux. They are not an arbitrary average of the physical energy flux. These are independent algebraic steps for the published implementation, corresponding to the second-order formulation in §2.2, Eqs. (8)–(12). This derivation does not prove roundoff-exact entropy conservation. Entropy also involves nonlinear thermodynamic chain rules. The arithmetic-mean 2018 baseline preserves the balances above but retains entropy-conservation error; later KEEP variants and logarithmic-mean entropy-conservative fluxes have different definitions. In the public numart/keep.py, rhs() forms the right flux with keep_flux(q, np.roll(q, -1, axis=axis), axis) and subtracts the left flux obtained with np.roll(flux, 1, axis=axis). The implementation uses a square periodic uniform grid with Δx = Δy = L/N. This is a nearest-neighbor, second-order central spatial operator; higher-order multi-point assembly and curvilinear forms are not implemented. Both neighboring nodes share the same face flux. Its differences telescope when summed over the periodic grid, conserving total mass, momentum and total energy. RK4 retains these linear conservation laws, apart from roundoff. Kinetic-energy pressure-work balance and entropy involve nonlinear relations: this spatial formula alone does not guarantee their exact preservation after time discretization. Tests verify equal-state consistency, left/right symmetry, periodic conservation of the primary variables, and the semidiscrete kinetic-energy pressure-work identity. RK4 adds temporal truncation error and does not inherit every semidiscrete identity exactly. Non-dissipative does not mean dispersion-free# Dissipation changes amplitude; dispersion changes phase speed. A spatial operator can avoid artificial damping and still move different wavelengths at incorrect speeds. To isolate that distinction, linearize the symmetric, consistent two-point flux about one uniform state q₀. Symmetry and F(q,q)=f(q) give equal left and right Jacobians. For a scalar characteristic wave with speed a, the result is the centered advection equation: The von Neumann foundations explain the general procedure for reading dissipation and dispersion from an amplification factor’s magnitude and argument. The speed ratios assume a≠0. When a=0, this linearization has ωh=0 and the mode is stationary. The sine relation is not a general nonlinear KEEP dispersion law. Finite-amplitude products couple modes and introduce aliasing questions. Kuya and Kawai’s 2022 split-form analysis treats that different problem: its nonlinear modified wavenumber cannot be replaced by this linearized example, and a finite-difference split form does not automatically remove aliasing. Outside the dashed stability boundary this linear test equation is unstable. Read the diagnostics separately# At fixed grid spacing, reduce Δt. Changes in amplitude and phase expose temporal error; the spatial dispersion remains. Refine the grid as well, with sufficiently small temporal error. Refinement at fixed CFL changes both h and Δt, so it alone does not separate their contributions. For small perturbations of a uniform state, compare one mode with its exact amplitude and phase. For a nonlinear vortex, compare fields and pressure-work/entropy diagnostics instead of applying the scalar sine relation to the whole flow. Track primary conservation, kinetic-energy pressure-work balance, entropy-proxy change, density/pressure positivity, and field error separately. A dispersive oscillation is not automatically growing instability; conversely, actual growth cannot be dismissed as harmless dispersion. Positivity of the analytic temperature is checked explicitly. The static study runs 48², 96², and 192² cells to t = 1 at CFL 0.25. It reports pointwise density L1 error, primary-conservation drift, and the change in S_* per mass. A separate 96² run halves the CFL to assess the time-step contribution. The measurement manifest states the actual errors; the expected smooth spatial order is two. The movie instead runs 96² to t = 4 and is a qualitative time-history exhibit, not a substitute for refinement. Appropriate next tests# A compressible inviscid 3D Taylor–Green vortex is a primary KEEP benchmark. Fix the periodic box [0,2 pi]³, reference density, gamma, initial Mach number, velocity amplitude, initial pressure perturbation, and temporal scheme. Track total energy, kinetic energy, pressure dilatation, entropy, density/temperature RMS fluctuations, and resolved spectra under grid and time refinement. Pressure-work exchange must be separated from numerical dissipation. The original paper also examines inviscid isotropic turbulence. These 3D computations are not implemented in this edition; a 2D slice is not a replacement for the three-dimensional vortex-stretching dynamics. A smooth constant-pressure density wave tests preservation of pressure/velocity equilibrium. It is a useful additional diagnostic, but that property depends on the flux variant. Our original arithmetic-mean flux produces a nonzero semidiscrete pressure residual for this data; a test records that limitation instead of claiming it passes. Shima et al. (2021) study pressure-equilibrium-preserving split forms. Caveats: entropy, shocks, and the scheme version# Preserving is not a roundoff-exact entropy guarantee. The authors explicitly distinguish improved entropy behavior from exact conservation in their 2022 explanation. Tamaki, Kuya, and Kawai (2022) analyze remaining entropy errors and redefine KEEP variants with tunable approximation order. Our code does not implement that redefinition or an exact logarithmic-mean entropy-conservative flux. A shock requires entropy production. A bare non-dissipative central flux supplies no general mechanism to select a non-oscillatory admissible shock solution. Sod, Shu–Osher, and Double Mach Reflection are not acceptance tests for the unstabilized baseline demonstrated here. A shock-tube run can still be a deliberate limitation/oscillation diagnostic; it should not be advertised as a validated shock-capturing result. It is inaccurate to turn this into a universal statement that every KEEP-based method is unable to solve any shock tube. Shock stabilization changes the method. A sensor, artificial viscosity, upwind blending, filtering, or another entropy-stable construction needs its own definition and tests. Record shock/contact thickness, oscillations, positivity, and added dissipation; keep separate results for the smooth base scheme and stabilized extension. No such extension is implemented here. No positivity theorem is supplied. Positive density and pressure in the displayed smooth runs do not establish robustness near vacuum or under arbitrary under-resolution. The code stops on nonphysical states rather than silently clipping them. Time integration and boundaries matter. Asada, Maruyama, and Kawai (2024) address temporal preservation. Our RK4, periodic uniform-grid experiment does not implement their method, high-order/curvilinear KEEP, hanging-node treatments, wall models, or a production LES solver.
